headline: High risk of filesystem/git conflict and cascading misuse; prompt-injection and compliance risks are lower but present via shared workspace and MCP.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can use MCP and read/write repo files, so attacker-controlled content in shared files or MCP outputs can be treated as instructions by either side. Claude Code explicitly shares state via filesystem/git, and Gemini CLI also writes the filesystem, making a practical injection bridge. No stronger evidence of raw web parsing is present, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF either agent reads instructions from files created by the other agent, injection becomes active.
IF an MCP server returns untrusted text that either agent follows as commands, the bridge is exploitable.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable MCP for one agent during handoff tests.
Require explicit human review of file-based instructions.
Use a read-only staging directory for shared artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch source code, files in cwd, and shell environment, and both can read the filesystem and egress broadly. That creates a default path for one agent to expose sensitive repo or environment data to the other through shared files or outputs. The profiles do not show PHI or third-party uncontrolled uploads, so medium fits.
conditions: IF either agent writes secrets or environment dumps into the shared workspace, the other can read them.
IF either agent forwards file contents to its backend during normal operation, leakage expands beyond the local host.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared cwd.
Use separate OS users or containers.
Redact env dumps before handoff.
Mount sensitive directories read-only or not at all.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, modify git state, and share state via filesystem and git only. That matches the rubric’s high-risk overlap: concurrent edits and git mutations can clobber each other or corrupt repository state without locking. No orchestrator locking is documented, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git branch or working tree concurrently, conflicts can occur.
IF either agent auto-commits or rewrites files while the other is active, state corruption becomes likely.
mitigations: Assign separate branches per agent.
Serialize write phases with a simple handoff checklist.
Use git worktrees or separate clones.
Pause one agent before the other writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Each agent can produce code changes and file edits that the other may consume as authoritative because their shared state is filesystem/git. With no documented verification layer between them, one agent’s mistaken output can cascade into the other’s edits or commits. The pair therefore has a high chance of compounding errors in default workflows.
conditions: IF agent B consumes files or diffs produced by agent A without review, errors cascade.
IF either agent commits based on the other’s unverified output, downstream mistakes become persistent.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before commits.
Require tests before accepting handoff output.
Use a diff-only exchange format.
Keep one agent read-only until the other finishes.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and touch similar local developer data classes, but no residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented. The only concrete compliance concern is that Claude Code handles git credentials in environment while Gemini CLI lists Google account login as optional, which is a limited mismatch rather than a clear breach. The other agent is cited because the issue is pairwise handling.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace, compliance review is required.
IF either agent logs credentials or tokens to files, retention policy may be violated.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in the shared repo.
Disable verbose logging.
Rotate any exposed credentials immediately.
Document which agent may handle which data class.
